hook_text: 42 grams went into the crucible. Only 20 can ever come out. Here's how the atoms set the ceiling.
clip_script: Run the actual problem in bakery language. You carry 42 grams of magnesium carbonate to the door. One mole of it costs 84 grams — so 42 grams is half a mole. Half a batch of raw material. Cross the recipe: one tray per batch. Half a batch in, half a tray out. Out through the far door: one mole of magnesium oxide weighs 40 grams, so half a mole is 20 grams. The oven can deliver at most 20 grams. And where did the other 22 grams go? Not lost — carried away as carbon dioxide gas. Add the two products: 20 plus 22 is 42, every gram accounted for. Atoms never vanish in a reaction; they change address.
visual_style: A crucible morphs into a bakery door; numbers walk through as little parcels — 42 g shrinks to 0,5 mol, crosses a bridge marked 1:1, exits as 20 g; a ghostly 22 g balloon floats away and the scale ticks back to 42.
mood: Confident reveal — a magic trick explained.
pacing: Steady walk through the three doors, then the mass-balance payoff lands with a satisfying click.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to predict every reaction's maximum before you ever light the burner.
